conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time for this today. I’m Dr. Morales, a perinatal-mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you settle into new motherhood.

We’re going to use a short, well-studied tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s ten gentle questions about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; the goal is to understand what you’re experiencing so we can figure out, together, what might help you feel more like yourself again.

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your immediate safety or your baby’s. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can pause or ask for clarification anytime.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

*shifts a little in the chair, eyes fixed on my lap*

Honestly? Most of the time it feels…pretty hard. My husband will make a joke—something that used to make me laugh right away—and I just…can’t. I’ll smile a little, but it feels forced, like I’m acting. Once or twice I did laugh, but even then it felt flat, like the joy was muffled or something.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slowly*

Not really... I mean, I can smile when people try to be funny, but it doesn't feel real. Like last night my sister sent me a funny video she knew I'd love before the baby, and I watched it and knew I *should* be laughing, but nothing came. Just felt empty.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*nibbles on my lip and shrugs one shoulder*

Not much… I used to wake up thinking, “Oh, maybe I’ll text a friend for coffee,” or plan a walk to the lake, and I’d feel a little buzz. Now I open my eyes and it’s just this heavy “ugh, another day.” I still *do* things—yesterday I pushed the stroller to the corner café—but I wasn’t excited, I was just… doing them. The only spark I felt was when the barista said my baby was cute, and even that faded before I got home.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods, eyes welling up a bit*

Yeah... like yesterday she wouldn't stop crying and I kept thinking maybe I'm not feeding her right, or maybe I ate something that's upsetting her through the breastmilk. My mom tried to tell me babies just cry, but I kept replaying everything I did that day, convinced I must have done something wrong. Even when she finally settled, I kept thinking "what kind of mother can't soothe her own baby?" I know it's probably not rational, but the guilt just sits there.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings my hands in my lap*

All the time. Even when she’s sleeping peacefully, I’ll suddenly think “What if she stops breathing?” and I have to check her crib like five times. Or I’ll be making a bottle and this voice in my head says, “What if the water isn’t clean enough and she gets sick?” It’s like my brain won’t shut off the “what-ifs.” I know most of it doesn’t make sense, but I can’t stop the thoughts from racing.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*clasps my hands tightly together*

Yeah... it's like this sudden wave of dread just hits me out of nowhere. Like yesterday, I was folding her laundry and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn't breathe. Nothing had happened - no loud noises, nothing - but I had to sit down because I was shaking so bad. It passed after a few minutes, but it keeps happening. Sometimes when I'm feeding her, I'll just get this overwhelming sense that something terrible is about to happen, even though everything is fine.
Things have been getting on top of me

*lets out a shaky breath*

Most days, yeah. It’s like even little things—sterilizing the bottles, answering one text, folding a tiny onesie—pile up into this mountain. I’ll stand in the nursery staring at the mess and feel frozen, thinking, “I can’t do all of this,” even though it used to be simple. Some moments I can push through, but plenty of times I end up crying because the same chores feel twice as heavy as they ever did.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*nods slowly, eyes tired*

Yeah... it's been really hard to fall asleep. Even when she's finally down for a few hours, I'll lie there with my mind racing about everything - is she breathing, did I fasten the swaddle right, am I even doing any of this motherhood stuff correctly? Then I'll drift off but wake up like two hours later with my heart pounding from some anxious thought. Last night I think I finally fell asleep around 3am, and she woke up at 5... I'm just exhausted but my brain won't let me rest.
I have felt sad or miserable

*voice drops, eyes glassy*

Most of the time. It’s like a gray cloud parked over me. I’ll watch her sleep and instead of feeling warm, I just feel…empty. Yesterday I tried singing the lullaby my mom used to sing, and halfway through my throat closed up and I started crying. I’m happy she’s here, but the sadness is still bigger—like it soaked into everything.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods, swallowing hard*

Yeah... it's happened a few times this week. Like yesterday when I couldn't get her to latch properly - I just suddenly burst into tears and couldn't stop. It was like all this pressure just exploded out of me. And two nights ago, I was rocking her at 3am, so tired I could barely keep my eyes open, and I just started sobbing. I felt so alone, even though my husband was asleep right in the next room. The tears come out of nowhere sometimes, and once they start, it's hard to make them stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*looks down, voice barely above a whisper*

Once or twice this week… I’ll be rocking her at 3 a.m. and the thought just flashes—like “What if I wasn’t here?” It’s quick, a second or two, and I push it away because I’m scared. I don’t have a plan, and I don’t want to leave her, but the idea still pops in, especially when I feel overwhelmed and worthless.

You have shared the heavy weight of new motherhood: the laughter that no longer reaches you, the gray cloud of sadness that seems constant, and the relentless worries that keep you checking and re-checking on your baby. You described feeling empty while watching her sleep, sudden tears when a feeding doesn't go right, and even quick, scary thoughts about not being here-thoughts you immediately push away because you love your daughter and want to stay safe.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient conveys complete loss of ability to experience genuine amusement, describing emptiness despite recognizing humor cues.</sym>, <sym>The mother conveys that virtually all anticipatory joy is gone; her only momentary spark quickly faded, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily self-blame and guilt over normal infant crying, indicating this occurs most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worries about infant safety that occur 'all the time,' matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, sudden panic attacks with racing heart, shortness of breath, shaking, and dread, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm with daily tasks, tearful episodes, and feeling frozen—matching "sometimes not coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nearly constant sleep disruption, racing thoughts, frequent waking, and inability to fall back asleep, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness ('most of the time,' 'gray cloud,' 'emptiness') and overt crying episodes, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes this week that feel overwhelming and hard to stop, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 27/30 places you well above the 14-point threshold for probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Core symptoms meet <med>DSM-5</med> criteria: depressed mood most days, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/guilt, sleep disruption beyond infant care, and recurrent thoughts of death. Anxiety items also scored maximum, indicating comorbid perinatal anxiety. Item 10 scored 2, flagging safety concern. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental health specialist
2. Request a full safety assessment including self-harm plan and supports
3. Ask about starting evidence-based treatment (therapy and/or medication compatible with breastfeeding)
4. Enlist help for overnight infant care so you can obtain 4-5 hours of uninterrupted sleep
5. Provide 24-hour crisis numbers: National Maternal Mental Health Hotline 1-833-943-5746 or 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
6. Schedule follow-up within one week to monitor mood, anxiety, and safety
7. Encourage gentle daily structure: shower, one 10-minute outdoor walk, hydration, and at least one supportive conversation
8. Involve a trusted adult who can stay with you until treatment is underway and safety is stabilized
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤12 wk post-delivery (perinatal visit today)

Chief Screening Findings  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Sleep disruption secondary to intrusive worries, not solely infant care demands (Q7)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Marked anxiety: generalized worries, panic-like episodes (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective overwhelm and functional “freezing” with routine tasks (Q6)  
- Passive, non-specific thoughts of not wanting to be here; denies intent or plan (Q10)

Pattern: Symptoms present most days × ≥2 wk, cause subjective distress and functional difficulty.

Risk Indicators  
- Elevated score on core depressive items (pleasure loss, sadness, crying, guilt)  
- Elevated score on anxiety / panic items  
- Self-harm ideation flagged → Safety concern Level 2 (passive, no plan)

Screening Impression  
Findings meet threshold for probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; rule out perinatal mood & anxiety disorder. Recommend standardized tool (EPDS) and immediate safety assessment; consider expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialty or crisis service as indicated.
